summary: Sets out requirements for Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO), a service that gives applications guidance when choosing among several equivalent hosts, such as peers in file sharing. The aim is to help applications pick well-placed sources while reducing wasted traffic on networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you can borrow a book from many friends, this is like a helper telling you which friend lives closest, so you do not walk across the whole town.

questions: how can applications choose the best peer
subtitle: What a service that advises applications on which peers or servers to pick must be able to do.

tldr.problem: Applications such as peer-to-peer file sharing often choose among many equivalent hosts but lack network topology and cost information, which providers may not want to disclose in detail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists numbered requirements (AR-1 to AR-46) for the ALTO client protocol, server discovery, and security and privacy, without defining a protocol itself.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document meant to be used when specifying, assessing or comparing ALTO protocols and implementations.

today: RFC 6708 is an Informational RFC from September 2012 and, according to the unit metadata, is not obsoleted or updated. It states requirements only, and the protocol and discovery specifications that meet them are separate documents.

sections.title: The Goal of ALTO
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) aims to give peer-to-peer (P2P) applications information that helps them select peers better. The RFC says it may help other applications too, for example by choosing among several servers or information replicas, or by selecting a media relay for NAT traversal. The aim is better performance or Quality of Experience while using less of the underlying network.

Applications usually cannot get this information themselves, because it depends on topology, operational costs or policies that the network provider does not want to disclose in detail. The ALTO functional entities do not relay user data. They may run on dedicated servers, as auxiliary processes in routers, or on trackers or super peers. The motivation comes from the problem statement in RFC 5693.
sections.eli5: Picking which friend to ask for a game is easier if a neighbor who knows the map gives you a hint. ALTO is that neighbor.

sections.title: Terms and Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC reuses terms from RFC 5693 (ALTO server, ALTO client, resource consumer, resource provider and others) and adds a few of its own.

  • Host-group descriptor: describes one or more hosts and where they are in the network, such as an IP address, a prefix or range, or an Autonomous System number.
  • Rating criterion: what "better" means in better-than-random peer selection, for example low topological distance.
  • Host-characteristics attribute: a property of a host other than its descriptor, such as whether its Internet access is flat rate.

The document does not mandate one architecture. It lists requirements for ALTO client protocols, server discovery, host-group descriptors, rating criteria and host-characteristics attributes, and leaves detailed protocol specification out of scope.
sections.eli5: It first agrees on the words: a way to name groups of computers, a rule for what counts as "better", and facts about each computer.

sections.title: Client Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Every ALTO client and server MUST implement an ALTO client protocol that carries queries and replies (AR-1) and provides operations and management support as outlined in RFC 5706 (AR-2).

Host-group descriptors: the protocol MUST support several descriptor types, clearly identified (AR-3, AR-4), including IPv4 and IPv6 address prefixes (AR-5). It MUST be extensible to other types (AR-6), and any other type must come with a way to map to IP prefixes (AR-7). Both sides need a way to say that a type is unsupported (AR-9, AR-10).

Rating criteria: a protocol specification MUST define a "relative operator's preference" criterion, which has no unit and need not reveal how ratings are computed (AR-11). The criteria set MUST be extensible (AR-12). Criteria must not target instantaneous congestion (AR-13), and applications MUST NOT rely solely on ALTO to avoid congestion (AR-14). The RFC explains that ALTO data may be updated rather infrequently, so it cannot replace TCP-like congestion control.

Extensibility: extensions MUST be backward compatible (AR-27) and the protocol MUST support versioning (AR-28).
sections.eli5: The rules say the helper must understand different ways of naming computers, must be able to grow new ideas, and must never replace the normal traffic-jam rules.

sections.title: Placement, Query Modes and Errors
sections.content:
An ALTO client may sit inside the resource consumer itself or inside a third party such as a resource directory or P2P tracker. The protocol MUST support both (AR-18, AR-19). It MUST allow the ALTO service to be run by someone other than the IP network operator (AR-20), let different providers' services coexist (AR-21), and work for clients behind a NAT (AR-26).

The RFC defines two query modes, and a protocol specification MUST specify at least one (AR-22) and SHOULD specify both (AR-23). If it specifies more than one, it MUST make at least one mandatory and provide a way to negotiate which to use.

Responses SHOULD carry version numbers or TTL attributes so caches can check validity (AR-24), and SHOULD say how far reuse is appropriate, from no reuse up to any consumer in the whole network (AR-25).

The protocol MUST use congestion-aware transport such as TCP (AR-29). A specification MUST give servers ways to signal overload (terminate the conversation, redirect to another server, or ask the client to throttle) and inability to answer (terminate, redirect, or retry later) (AR-30, AR-31). Servers are not obliged to use these mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The helper can sit in your own phone or in a middleman. If the helper is too busy, it must have a polite way to say "ask someone else" or "try again later".

sections.title: ALTO Server Discovery
sections.content:
Clients need a way to find ALTO servers. The RFC names two modes: resource consumer initiated discovery, where a client embedded in the consumer finds servers (AR-32), and third-party discovery, where a client in a resource directory finds servers for a remote consumer (AR-33). Both MUST work behind a NAT, including when the consumer being served is behind a NAT (AR-34 to AR-36).

Discovery mechanisms SHOULD reuse an existing mechanism, such as DNS-, DHCP- or PPP-based automatic configuration, and a single broad mechanism is preferred over several narrow ones (AR-37). They SHOULD return several servers (AR-38) and indicate preferences among them (AR-39).
sections.eli5: Before you can ask the helper, you need to know where it lives. The rules say finding it should use ways the network already has.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A client protocol specification MUST specify authentication of servers (AR-40) and of clients (AR-41), and encryption of messages (AR-42), or say how to use mechanisms from lower layers. It MUST support different levels of detail in queries and responses to protect user privacy (AR-44), and must protect against Denial-of-Service attacks (AR-46). A client may name the wanted resource, but the server MUST give good guidance even when the client leaves it out (AR-45). Clients need not limit redistribution of what they learn (AR-43).

Section 5 classifies information disclosure risks. For operators, the risks are excess disclosure to clients, disclosure to unauthorized parties, and collaborating clients combining responses. For users, the risks are what a server or a third party can infer about application behavior. The RFC says plain authentication and encryption do not help against clients forwarding data or colluding, so operators should only feed in data they do not consider sensitive in those cases. Users can reduce exposure with a proxy, a third-party client, a broader address range, or the target-independent query mode, with a possible loss of accuracy.
sections.eli5: The helper must check who is asking, keep messages private, and not learn too much about what you are up to.

The client's list of host-group descriptors, sorted by the rating criteria or enriched with attributes
